idiom_name: hand-written counted body: _Atomic refcount plus an atomically published snapshot pointer, writes serialised by a mutex
implementation_notes: C has no smart pointer and no destructor, so the whole structure is written out: a body struct carrying an _Atomic counter, an atomic snapshot pointer that readers load with atomic_load/atomic_load_explicit, and a mutex (mtx_t from <threads.h>, or pthread_mutex_t on POSIX) that serialises writers. Copies increment the count with atomic_fetch_add and release with atomic_fetch_sub, freeing the body when the count reaches one; because the body is published atomically, a reader does not need the count at all, only a guarantee that the body it loaded stays alive - which is exactly where C is weakest: without a counted reference on the read path you need hazard pointers or an epoch/grace-period scheme, and with a counted reference you need every read path to take and drop it. Note that the primitives themselves are optional: a freestanding implementation may define __STDC_NO_ATOMICS__ or __STDC_NO_THREADS__, in which case the pattern degrades to compiler intrinsics plus pthreads. If writes are not rare, drop the whole structure and use one pthread_rwlock_t or mutex around a mutable body.
pitfalls: The count and the pointer are two different protections: an atomic count alone does not make a plain pointer read safe while another thread swaps the pointer, so the published pointer must itself be atomic (or guarded), or the reader has a data race.

The load and the dereference are not one operation: a body can be freed by the last releaser while a reader is still inside it, unless the read path takes its own reference, or a grace period (epoch/hazard pointer) guarantees the reader is done.

Half of the primitives are optional and the default memory order is the most expensive: __STDC_NO_ATOMICS__ and __STDC_NO_THREADS__ can remove the C11 headers entirely, and atomic_fetch_add's sequential-consistency default costs a full barrier where memory_order_acq_rel/release would do.
